title: Legal & Ethical — Confidentiality, HIPAA Exceptions & Tarasoff (Set 5)
subtitle: Protected health information, permitted disclosures (treatment/payment/operations), authorization & release of information, the legal exceptions to confidentiality (duty to warn/Tarasoff, mandated abuse reporting, danger to self, court order, communicable-disease reporting), need-to-know access, and everyday breach prevention
scenario: Protecting client confidentiality under HIPAA and California law: what may be shared and with whom, the specific legal exceptions that permit or require disclosure, and how to prevent everyday privacy breaches.

steps.q: Under HIPAA, 'protected health information' (PHI) refers to:

opts.text: Individually identifiable health information, including the client's diagnosis, treatment, and the fact that they are a client
opts.rat: PHI is any individually identifiable health information—including that a person is even receiving care—and it must be safeguarded.

opts.text: Only the client's written medical chart
opts.rat: PHI includes spoken, electronic, and written information, not just the paper chart.

opts.text: Only laboratory and imaging results
opts.rat: PHI covers far more than test results—demographics, diagnoses, and the fact of treatment are all protected.

opts.text: Information that is safe to post publicly once the name is removed
opts.rat: Removing a name alone does not make details shareable; other identifiers can still reveal who the client is.

steps.q: Without specific written authorization, PHI may generally still be used or shared for:

opts.text: Treatment, payment, and health-care operations
opts.rat: HIPAA permits disclosures for treatment, payment, and routine health-care operations without a separate authorization; other uses generally require the client's written consent.

opts.text: Posting an interesting case on social media
opts.rat: Sharing on social media is never a permitted disclosure, regardless of intent.

opts.text: Telling a curious neighbor about the client
opts.rat: Personal curiosity is never a lawful reason to disclose PHI.

opts.text: Any purpose, as long as staff mean well
opts.rat: Good intentions do not authorize disclosure; the purpose must be legally permitted.

steps.q: A client tells staff a specific, credible plan to seriously harm a named person after discharge. Under the Tarasoff 'duty to protect,' the treatment team must:

opts.text: Take reasonable steps to protect the intended victim, which may include warning them and/or notifying authorities
opts.rat: When a client makes a serious threat of violence against a reasonably identifiable victim, the duty to protect can require warning the victim and/or notifying law enforcement—this overrides ordinary confidentiality.

opts.text: Keep the threat completely confidential no matter what
opts.rat: A serious, identifiable threat is a recognized exception to confidentiality; staying silent could violate the duty to protect.

opts.text: Wait to see whether the client acts on the threat
opts.rat: Waiting fails the duty to protect; reasonable protective steps must be taken.

opts.text: Discharge the client immediately to end responsibility
opts.rat: Discharging does not fulfill—and may worsen—the duty to protect the potential victim.

steps.q: The technician suspects a child is being abused based on a client's disclosure. Regarding confidentiality, the technician:

opts.text: Is a mandated reporter and must report the suspected abuse, which is a lawful exception to confidentiality
opts.rat: Suspected child (and elder/dependent-adult) abuse must be reported by mandated reporters; the law requires disclosure and confidentiality does not apply.

opts.text: Must keep it confidential because the client shared it privately
opts.rat: Mandated reporting of suspected abuse is a legal duty that overrides confidentiality.

opts.text: Should investigate and confirm the abuse before telling anyone
opts.rat: Mandated reporters report reasonable suspicion; they do not need to prove abuse first.

opts.text: Should report only if the client gives permission
opts.rat: Client permission is not required to make a mandated abuse report.

steps.q: Two technicians discuss a client's case by name in a crowded elevator. This is:

opts.text: A breach of confidentiality; client care should not be discussed where others can overhear
opts.rat: Discussing identifiable client information in public areas risks disclosure to unauthorized people and is a confidentiality breach.

opts.text: Acceptable because they are both staff members
opts.rat: Even between staff, client information may only be shared on a need-to-know basis and never where others can overhear.

opts.text: Acceptable as long as they speak quietly
opts.rat: The public setting itself is the problem; lowering the voice does not make it appropriate.

opts.text: Acceptable because the client is not present
opts.rat: The client's absence does not make public discussion of their information appropriate.

steps.q: Posting about a client on personal social media is:

opts.text: Never appropriate, even without naming the client, because details can still identify them
opts.rat: Social media posts about clients—named or not—can breach confidentiality and violate policy and law; they are never appropriate.

opts.text: Fine if the client's name is left out
opts.rat: Omitting the name does not remove other identifying details; the post can still breach confidentiality.

opts.text: Fine if the post is set to 'friends only'
opts.rat: Privacy settings do not make disclosing PHI acceptable.

opts.text: Fine if it is meant to celebrate the client's progress
opts.rat: Positive intent does not authorize disclosing client information publicly.

steps.q: A client's adult sibling calls the unit and asks for details about the client's condition. The technician should:

opts.text: Not disclose information without verifying the caller and confirming the client has authorized that disclosure
opts.rat: Being a relative does not by itself grant access; disclosure requires the client's authorization and identity verification.

opts.text: Share the full update because it is a close family member
opts.rat: Family relationship alone does not authorize disclosure of PHI.

opts.text: Confirm the diagnosis but withhold the treatment plan
opts.rat: Any PHI disclosure still requires authorization; partial disclosure is still a disclosure.

opts.text: Give the information only if the caller sounds worried
opts.rat: Emotional tone is not a basis for disclosing PHI.

steps.q: Before the facility sends a client's records to another treatment provider at the client's request, it generally needs:

opts.text: A signed authorization/release-of-information from the client (or legal representative)
opts.rat: Releasing records to an outside party typically requires a valid signed authorization specifying what may be shared and with whom.

opts.text: Only a verbal 'okay' shouted across the room
opts.rat: A casual verbal statement is not a valid release; written authorization is required.

opts.text: Nothing, since the records belong to the client
opts.rat: Even though the client controls disclosure, a documented authorization is still required to release records.

opts.text: Approval from the client's employer
opts.rat: The employer has no authority over the client's health records.

steps.q: A client asks to see a copy of their own medical record. The best response is to:

opts.text: Explain that clients generally have the right to access their records and follow the facility's process to arrange it
opts.rat: Clients have a right to access their own health information; the technician follows facility procedure to route the request appropriately.

opts.text: Refuse because clients are never allowed to see their records
opts.rat: Clients do have a right of access to their own records; a flat refusal is incorrect.

opts.text: Hand over the entire chart immediately without any process
opts.rat: Access is provided through the proper process, not by handing over the chart on the spot.

opts.text: Tell the client to file a lawsuit to obtain the record
opts.rat: A lawsuit is unnecessary; records access follows a normal request process.

steps.q: A caller says, 'I'm the client's spouse—just tell me if they're there.' Confirming that the person is even a client:

opts.text: Would itself disclose PHI, so it should not be confirmed without proper authorization/verification
opts.rat: The very fact that someone is receiving care is protected; acknowledging their presence without authorization is a disclosure.

opts.text: Is harmless because it does not reveal a diagnosis
opts.rat: Confirming that a person is a client is itself PHI, even without a diagnosis.

opts.text: Is required whenever a spouse asks
opts.rat: Spousal status does not automatically authorize disclosure.

opts.text: Is acceptable if the caller knows the client's birthday
opts.rat: Knowing a personal detail does not establish authorization to receive PHI.

steps.q: The facility receives a valid court order to release a specific client's records. The facility:

opts.text: May release the information as legally required by the court order
opts.rat: A valid court order is a recognized legal exception; the facility complies with what the order specifies.

opts.text: Must refuse because records are always confidential
opts.rat: A lawful court order is an exception that permits disclosure.

opts.text: Should release the records only if the client agrees
opts.rat: A valid court order does not require the client's separate agreement.

opts.text: Should release every client's records, not just the one named
opts.rat: Only the information specified in the order is released—not other clients' records.

steps.q: Certain communicable diseases must be reported to public health authorities. This illustrates that:

opts.text: Public-health reporting laws are a lawful exception that can require disclosure despite confidentiality
opts.rat: Mandatory disease-reporting laws protect the public and are a recognized exception to individual confidentiality.

opts.text: Confidentiality can never be broken for any reason
opts.rat: Several legal exceptions exist, including public-health reporting.

opts.text: Staff may report anything they wish about any client
opts.rat: Only what the reporting law requires is disclosed, to the proper authority.

opts.text: Reporting is optional and up to each employee
opts.rat: Reportable-disease disclosure is a legal requirement, not optional.

steps.q: A client states a clear intent to end their own life. Regarding confidentiality, the team:

opts.text: May share necessary information with the treatment team and appropriate parties to keep the client safe
opts.rat: Imminent danger to self is a recognized exception; relevant information is shared as needed to protect the client's safety.

opts.text: Must keep the statement secret to preserve trust
opts.rat: Client safety takes priority; the information is shared with those who need it to protect the client.

opts.text: Should tell no one until the next scheduled meeting
opts.rat: A safety threat requires prompt communication, not waiting for a meeting.

opts.text: Should post it in the chart but tell no staff
opts.rat: The team must be informed so protective action can be taken.

steps.q: A technician is curious and looks up the record of a well-known person who is a client on another unit—someone not in the technician's care. This is:

opts.text: A privacy violation; staff may access only the records of clients they are caring for, on a need-to-know basis
opts.rat: Access is limited to those with a legitimate treatment need; accessing records out of curiosity violates privacy rules regardless of who the client is.

opts.text: Acceptable because the technician works at the facility
opts.rat: Employment does not grant access to records without a care-related need.

opts.text: Acceptable because the person is a public figure
opts.rat: Public figures have the same privacy protections as any other client.

opts.text: Acceptable as long as nothing is shared with others
opts.rat: Unauthorized access itself is the violation, even if nothing is further shared.

steps.q: When client cases are discussed for teaching or training purposes, the technician should:

opts.text: De-identify the information and share only what is necessary for the educational purpose
opts.rat: Removing identifiers and limiting detail lets staff learn from cases without breaching confidentiality.

opts.text: Use the client's full name so the example is clear
opts.rat: Using identifiers is unnecessary for teaching and breaches confidentiality.

opts.text: Include the client's room number and photo
opts.rat: These are identifiers that should never be included.

opts.text: Discuss the case openly in the public cafeteria
opts.rat: A public setting risks disclosure regardless of teaching intent.

steps.q: A reasonable safeguard to protect electronic PHI at a shared workstation is to:

opts.text: Log off or lock the screen when stepping away and never share login credentials
opts.rat: Logging off and keeping credentials private prevent unauthorized access to electronic records.

opts.text: Leave the record open so the next staff member saves time
opts.rat: An open, unattended record can be viewed by unauthorized people.

opts.text: Write the password on a sticky note on the monitor
opts.rat: Posting a password defeats access controls and is a serious security lapse.

opts.text: Share one login among the whole team for convenience
opts.rat: Shared logins remove accountability and violate security policy.

steps.q: 'Privileged communication' between a client and their therapist generally means that:

opts.text: The client typically holds the privilege and controls whether that protected information is disclosed
opts.rat: Privileged communication protects certain client–provider disclosures; the privilege generally belongs to the client, who decides on release, subject to legal exceptions.

opts.text: The therapist may share the information with anyone at will
opts.rat: The therapist cannot freely disclose privileged information; the client controls it.

opts.text: The information can never be disclosed under any circumstance
opts.rat: Legal exceptions (such as duty to warn or a court order) can still apply.

opts.text: Privilege belongs to the facility, not the client
opts.rat: The privilege generally belongs to the client, not the institution.

steps.q: Before faxing or emailing documents that contain PHI, the technician should:

opts.text: Verify the correct recipient and use a secure method (for example, a confidentiality cover sheet or encrypted email)
opts.rat: Confirming the recipient and using secure transmission reduce the risk of sending PHI to the wrong person.

opts.text: Send it to a general office number to save time
opts.rat: Sending PHI to an unverified or general destination risks disclosure to the wrong people.

opts.text: Assume any number in the directory is fine
opts.rat: The recipient must be verified; assumptions cause misdirected PHI.

opts.text: Include extra clients' information in case it is useful
opts.rat: Only the minimum necessary information for the intended recipient should be sent.

steps.q: If a technician realizes a confidentiality breach has occurred (for example, records were sent to the wrong person), the best action is to:

opts.text: Report the breach promptly through the facility's required process
opts.rat: Prompt reporting lets the facility take required steps to contain the breach and meet legal obligations.

opts.text: Say nothing and hope no one notices
opts.rat: Concealing a breach can cause further harm and violates policy and law.

opts.text: Delete the records to erase the evidence
opts.rat: Destroying records is improper and can compound the violation.

opts.text: Handle it privately without telling anyone
opts.rat: Breaches must be reported through the proper channel, not handled silently.

steps.q: Which situation is a lawful EXCEPTION that can permit or require breaking confidentiality?

opts.text: A serious threat of harm to an identifiable person (duty to warn/protect)
opts.rat: A credible, serious threat against an identifiable victim triggers the duty to protect—a recognized exception to confidentiality.

opts.text: A coworker being curious about a client's story
opts.rat: Curiosity is never a lawful basis to disclose PHI.

opts.text: A friend asking how a mutual acquaintance is doing
opts.rat: Personal inquiries do not authorize disclosure.

opts.text: Wanting to share an interesting case online
opts.rat: Sharing cases publicly is a breach, not a lawful exception.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Legal & Ethical (LPS Act & Patient Rights) — confidentiality and its exceptions. Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references. HIPAA concepts (protected health information; permitted treatment/payment/operations disclosures; authorization/release-of-information; client right of access; minimum-necessary/need-to-know) and the recognized exceptions to confidentiality — duty to warn/protect (Tarasoff, a California doctrine), mandated abuse reporting, imminent danger to self, valid court order, and mandatory communicable-disease reporting — are stated at an introductory level and marked for faculty confirmation against current California law and facility policy. Extends the intro confidentiality items in legal-core-01/02 and the HIPAA minimum-necessary item in legal-core-03. No specific statutes, code sections, timeframes, or dollar penalties are asserted. Pending faculty review.
